The Atlantic anchoveta Cetengraulis edentulus is a small engraulid that supports significant coastal fisheries along the Caribbean and South American Atlantic coasts. Early life history begins with the release of pelagic eggs, which hatch into yolk-sac larvae after a brief incubation period. Under the warm thermal conditions typical of its tropical spawning grounds, at a constant water temperature of 27.4 °C [T = 27.4 °C], which closely matches the species preferred reproductive environment, the age at birth is only 4 days [ab = 4 days]. This rapid embryonic development is consistent with the high metabolic demands of warm-water clupeiforms. The yolk-sac larva emerging from the chorion at eclosion carries a mass of just 0.00027 grams [Wwb = 0.00027 grams], a value derived from the egg diameter of approximately 0.8 mm. This minuscule initial size imposes high vulnerability to planktonic predation during the endotrophic phase, which lasts until the completion of yolk absorption and the onset of first exogenous feeding.

Sexual maturation in this species occurs at a relatively modest body size compared to other clupeiforms of similar ecology. Field surveys and gonad histology studies consistently indicate that the total length at puberty, the point at which 50 percent of individuals display active gametogenesis, is 13.7 centimeters [Lp = 13.7 centimeters]. Fish attaining this length are typically transitioning from the juvenile stage into reproductively viable adults. The wet weight at puberty corresponding to this size threshold, as estimated from length-weight regressions, is approximately 23 grams [Wwp = approximately 23 grams]. This relationship between size and maturity suggests that Atlantic anchoveta prioritizes early reproductive onset over extended somatic growth, a pattern common among short-lived, highly fecund small pelagics operating under high natural mortality regimes.

Reproductive output in Cetengraulis edentulus is substantial, reflecting the species role as a classic r-selected forage fish. Under the stable thermal conditions of 27.4 °C [T = 27.4 °C], which prevail during the prolonged spawning season, individual females can produce up to 11,018 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = up to 11,018 eggs per spawning event]. This high fecundity per event is complemented by a spawning frequency that may reach approximately 2 spawning events per year [F_R_i = approximately 2 spawning events per year]. The combination of elevated batch fecundity with such rapid serial spawning translates into an extraordinary annual reproductive potential, allowing the population to quickly rebound from heavy fishing pressure or environmental perturbations. The maximum recorded total length for this species is 20.5 centimeters [Li = 20.5 centimeters], representing the upper bound of individual somatic growth. Achieving this size requires sustained foraging on planktonic resources and favorable oceanographic conditions.

The ultimate wet weight of adult Atlantic anchoveta, based on the maximum published body mass for the species, reaches approximately 140.58 grams [Wwi = approximately 140.58 grams]. This value was recorded from a particularly large individual sampled in the southern Caribbean, and it likely represents close to the asymptotic mass under optimal feeding conditions. In contrast, the mass at puberty, which is roughly 23 grams [Wwp = roughly 23 grams], indicates that individuals invest in reproduction well before approaching their maximum size, a life-history tactic that buffers population-level reproductive output against high adult mortality rates. Body condition indices among gravid females show significant seasonal variation linked to plankton blooms, with the heaviest individuals typically recorded during the upwelling season when prey availability peaks.

Longevity data for this species, collected from otolith increment analysis and tag-recapture studies conducted at the species preferred thermal regime of 27.4 °C [T = 27.4 °C], indicate a maximum lifespan of approximately 3 years [am = approximately 3 years]. Only a very small fraction of the population survives beyond this age, as natural mortality and fishing pressure combine to produce a steeply declining survivorship curve. Historical records from the 1960s provide the basis for the maximum published weight of 140.58 grams [Wwi = 140.58 grams], while more recent surveys confirm that individuals exceeding 20.5 centimeters [Li = 20.5 centimeters] in total length are exceptionally rare. Comparative studies with related engraulids such as the Peruvian anchoveta highlight how these life-history parameters are finely tuned to the thermal and trophic dynamics of tropical coastal ecosystems.
